summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, legislates on these questions itself, and United Kingdom statutes reach the island only by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have that new gender recognised.

The Equality Act 2017, which received royal assent on 18 July 2017 and was largely brought into force on 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024; the Isle of Man was the first part of the British Isles to prohibit the practice.

Partner recognition is established. Civil partnerships became available to same-sex couples under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) on 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage took effect on 22 July 2016 after royal assent on 19 July 2016. A civil partnership converts into a marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force, indicating routine registration rather than discretionary approval.

Parental recognition is narrower than the marriage position. Full joint and stepchild adoption has been open to same-sex couples since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates for children born through IVF or surrogacy, and no Manx law acknowledges surrogacy. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law would meet that gap.

Sexual-conduct law on the island has been gender-neutral since the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which set a single age of consent of sixteen for all sexual conduct regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

A hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status was put to community consultation in July 2022. The sources reviewed do not record its enactment.

Isle of Man Prison (Jurby), the island's only functioning prison, opened as a fully operational facility on 14 August 2008 and is run by the Isle of Man Prison Service. It holds separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders, vulnerable prisoners and a segregation unit. No birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
The 2021 Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed before 1992 on the model of the United Kingdom's 2017 Alan Turing law. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 the police commissioner formally apologised on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.

Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men where conduct was under sixteen or not in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral.

Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3).

The House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment on 30 November 2005 protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran; the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) made dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation unlawful from 1 September 2006.

Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, preceding the 2016 Marriage and Civil Partnership Act.
localsOnly:
The Equality Act 2017 defines sexual orientation to include attraction to the same sex, the opposite sex, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, and lists it as a protected characteristic alongside gender reassignment.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) is the domestic mechanism by which Manx residents change their legal gender and have the new gender recognised.

Residents convicted of historical gay sex offences before 1992 fall within the pardon enacted by the Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021, in force 1 July 2022.

Same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011, and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates for children born through IVF or surrogacy and no Manx law acknowledges surrogacy.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed do not record enactment of the hate crime bill consulted on in July 2022; whether it has since passed is unresolved on this record.

No birth-sex-versus-identity prison placement rule, trans-specific unit, or trans-specific solitary or segregation practice is documented for Isle of Man Prison (Jurby); the absence of a documented rule is not evidence that no such practice exists.

No entry, visa, or border-screening treatment specific to transgender travellers is documented in the sources reviewed for the Isle of Man.

No trans-specific violence or killing statistics for the Isle of Man appear in the sources reviewed, so no trans-specific rate can be stated or compared against the island's general homicide rate.
